To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the typicality of conjunctive concepts depends on the typicality of the constituent concepts and on the relative frequency of the conjunctions, (2) the membership of conjunctive classes is overextended, and (3) the typicality and class membership of conjunctives are determined by the same process.
the overextended judgments of conjunctive concept typicality are due to the fact that people use a unitary prototype to judge the typicality of both single and conjuctive concepts.

people overextend conjunctive concepts, that there is an asymmetry in the influence of constituent concepts on conjunctive concept typicality and membership, and that these results can be explained by a unitary model that treats the representation of conjunctive concepts and the representation of single concepts as essentially the same.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the representation of conjunctive concepts and the process by which people form judgments of membership in them.
the nature of the mental representation of conjunctive concepts.
how people represent concepts and how they use those representations in judgment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of this research are consistent with the hypothesis that people form conjunctive concepts by combining the intensions of the constituent concepts to form a composite, conjunctive concept intension, and that the intension of the conjunctive concept is then used in a unitary way to make judgments of both typicality and class membership.
the conjunctive concept is a prototype that is a combination of the prototypes of the constituent concepts.

a conjunction such as sports which are games is represented as having an intension which specifies that it includes all and only the members of sports which are games, and a prototype which is a composite of the prototypes of sports and games.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the conjunctive concept prototype is a weighted average of the intensions of its constituents, with the weights determined by the relative typicality of the constituents.

people's intensions for the constituent concepts are not combined in the way that the conjunction rules would predict, but that the intensional representations are combined in the same way as they are for single concepts.
the prototype theory of concepts (Rosch & Mervis, 1975; Rosch, Mervis, Gray, Johnson, & Boyes-Braem, 1976) provides an elegant and parsimonious account of concept representation and concept use.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are no special processes for conjunctive concept formation, and that conjunctive concepts are no more complex than single concepts.
people's intuitions of typicality and membership in conjunctive classes are not independent, but instead are both governed by the same underlying model.
the typicality and the membership judgments are both determined by the same prototype.
